summary: Question: will the elevated post-2020 macro uncertainty persist and what should investors do. Method: JLN macro uncertainty index persistence regression, Fed-tradeoff and market-disagreement evidence, decade Sharpe ratios and SG Trend in drawdowns. Conclusion: uncertainty likely stays high, so diversify beyond equities toward bonds, commodities, trend following and global macro.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: We can quantify macroeconomic uncertainty by measuring the degree to which the economy has become more or less predictable over time.
claims.claim: Macro uncertainty is measured as how unpredictable the economy is: small gaps between data releases and their predicted values mean low uncertainty, large gaps mean high.
claims.exact_rule: uncertainty = size of forecast errors of macro releases
claims.testable: yes - construction given in later chunk

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: whether elevated uncertainty is likely to persist, or should we instead expect a return to the low uncertainty environment of the 2010s?
claims.claim: Key question of the note: will elevated macro uncertainty persist or revert to the 2010s low-uncertainty regime, and what follows for traditional assets and alternatives.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: inflation continues to be well above target, the federal funds rate is at its highest level since before the global financial crisis, and further rate hikes may be necessary.
claims.claim: Backdrop as of May 2023: inflation well above target, funds rate highest since pre-GFC, unemployment lowest in over 50 years, banks hit by compressed margins and shrinking deposits.
claims.reported_result: As of May 2023 (note dated Q2 2023)
claims.conditions: Dated backdrop; the thesis is conditioned on it

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: The authors use a high-dimensional statistical factor model to produce one-month-ahead forecasts of 132 macroeconomic series.
claims.claim: JLN macro uncertainty index builds one-month-ahead factor-model forecasts of 132 macro series.
claims.exact_rule: forecast 132 macro series one month ahead with a high-dimensional factor model
claims.data_needed: Jurado-Ludvigson-Ng (2015) macro uncertainty index, publicly available on Ludvigson's website; monthly from July 1960

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: The uncertainty index is the common component of the conditional volatility of the forecast errors at each point in time. It is standardized to have a mean of zero and standard deviation of one.
claims.claim: JLN is the common component of the conditional volatility of forecast errors, standardised to mean 0 and sd 1 (so values are z-scores).
claims.exact_rule: common component of conditional volatility of forecast errors; z-scored (mean 0, sd 1)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Macro uncertainty has indeed been exceptionally elevated throughout the 2020s. It peaked in the first half of 2020 and is currently at levels not seen since the 1980s, save for during the global financial crisis.
claims.claim: JLN has been exceptionally high in the 2020s, peaking in H1 2020 and now above anything since the 1980s except the GFC; the 2010s were consistently below average.
claims.reported_result: Figure 1 (July 1960-Dec 2022): peak about 5.3 in 2020, about 4.1 in 2008-09, about 3.1 around 1980-81, about 2.2 around 1974-75; about 1.3 at end-2022 (read from chart)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Historically, macro uncertainty tends to be very persistent—on the scale of quarters and years, not weeks and
claims.claim: Macro uncertainty is very persistent over quarters and years, with high and low periods clustering together, so elevated readings should last.
claims.reported_result: Quantified in the AR(1) regression in Figure/section on persistence (C03)
claims.direction: elevated uncertainty now implies elevated uncertainty later

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: During months in which the JLN index exceeds one, average annualized excess returns for U.S. equities is -16 percent and average annualized realized volatility is 21 percent,
claims.claim: When JLN exceeds 1, US equities average -16%/yr excess return and 21% realized vol, versus +6% excess return and 12% vol in all other months.
claims.exact_rule: months with JLN > 1 vs all other months
claims.data_needed: JLN index; US equity excess returns (vs cash) and realized volatility
claims.reported_result: JLN>1: -16% annualized excess return, 21% realized vol; other months: +6% and 12%. Sample not stated (JLN from 1960); no t-stat reported
claims.direction: high uncertainty -> lower equity returns and higher vol
claims.conditions: descriptive, contemporaneous months, not a forecast test
claims.testable: yes - coded from public data; sample not stated

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: taking the absolute value of the difference between actual and forecasted values for year-on-year real GDP growth, CPI inflation, and industrial production growth, and averaging across these three releases each quarter
claims.claim: Robustness proxy for JLN: quarterly average absolute forecast error of y/y real GDP growth, CPI inflation and industrial production growth.
claims.exact_rule: mean over {real GDP y/y, CPI inflation, industrial production growth} of |actual - forecast|, per quarter
claims.data_needed: Actual and forecast values for those three releases (forecast source not named)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Nevertheless, the two indices track each other well, with a correlation 0.7.
claims.claim: The simple forecast-error measure and JLN have a correlation of 0.7, which the author uses to confirm JLN is reasonable.
claims.reported_result: Correlation 0.7 between JLN and simple measure (sample not stated)
claims.testable: yes - computable if forecast source known

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: By virtue of equating uncertainty to the conditional volatility of forecast errors, as opposed to the magnitude of realized forecast errors, JLN is more theoretically appealing.
claims.claim: JLN is preferred over the simple measure because it uses conditional volatility of forecast errors rather than realized error size, and covers many more releases.
claims.conditions: Authors say JLN is also empirically more appealing for using a much larger set of releases

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: links it to the below average performance of trend following strategies during that decade.
claims.claim: Low macro volatility in the 2010s is linked by the author to below-average trend-following performance in that decade (separate AQR note).

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: While asset returns are notoriously difficult to forecast, asset volatility tends to be persistent and, therefore, much more predictable.
claims.claim: Volatility is persistent and thus more predictable than returns, motivating a test of whether macro uncertainty is persistent the same way.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.claim: One-month AR(1) of JLN has slope 0.98 and R2 97%: today's index is almost the best forecast of next month's.
claims.exact_rule: JLN(t+1) = 0.98 x JLN(t), no intercept shown, monthly
claims.reported_result: Slope 0.98, R2 = 97% (sample presumably 1960-2022; intercept not reported)
claims.conditions: Footnote 4: R2 equals slope squared, so it only restates persistence

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: If the JLN index is 1.0 this month, our best prediction is it will be 0.98 next month, and 0.98 12 ≈ 0.8 next year.
claims.claim: Implied decay: JLN of 1.0 forecast to 0.98 next month and about 0.8 in a year (0.98^12).

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: The half- life of shocks to macro uncertainty is around 4 years.
claims.claim: Author states the half-life of shocks to macro uncertainty is around 4 years.
claims.reported_result: Half-life around 4 years as stated; note that ln(0.5)/ln(0.98) is about 34 months (2.9 years), so the stated 4 years does not follow from the 0.98 slope (reader check; may use a different estimate)
claims.conditions: Inconsistent with 0.98 monthly slope; unspecified how 4 years was obtained

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: As of the end of 2022, the JLN macro uncertainty index stands at 1.27, which is the 88 percentile relative to history
claims.claim: As of end-2022 JLN = 1.27 (88th percentile); persistence implies a one-year forecast of 1.06 (85th percentile) and two-year 0.89 (84th).
claims.reported_result: End-2022 JLN 1.27 (88th pct); 1-yr forecast 1.06 (85th pct); 2-yr forecast 0.89 (84th pct)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Don’t be shocked by the extremely high R 2 . In this simple time series model the R 2 is simply the slope coefficient squared. So, the high R 2 simply means the JLN measure is very persistent.
claims.claim: Footnote: the 97% R2 is just the squared slope (0.98^2), so it carries no extra information beyond persistence.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Statistical forecasts are far from sure things. Perhaps “this time is different” and macro uncertainty will rapidly recede?
claims.claim: Author concedes the persistence forecast could fail, then turns to the economic backdrop for two catalysts that argue against a rapid recession of uncertainty.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: 2. Market-implied expectations of key economic variables disagree materially with policymaker and economist forecasts, and even disagree across markets.
claims.claim: Two catalysts for persistent uncertainty: (1) delayed effect of rate hikes plus central bank employment/inflation tradeoffs; (2) disagreement between market-implied and policymaker/economist forecasts and across markets.
claims.testable: partly - one tested (tradeoffs), one by example

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Monetary policy influences economic activity primarily through its impact on interest rate-sensitive components of demand—e.g., business and housing investment, demand for consumer durables, etc.
claims.claim: Rate hikes work through rate-sensitive demand (business and housing investment, consumer durables) and through bank lending (higher rates and a flatter curve compress net interest margins and reduce credit); these effects take time.
claims.direction: tightening -> weaker activity with a lag

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: monetary actions affect economic conditions only after a lag that is both long and variable.
claims.claim: Milton Friedman: monetary policy acts with a long and variable lag, so the effect of 2022-23 hikes is still to come.
claims.conditions: Footnote 5 says the idea that transmission is faster now confuses fast asset-price reaction with real-economy effect; the wealth effect on consumption is 'pennies on the dollar'

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: the impact of changes in liquid asset wealth on consumption is pennies on the dollar, and this “wealth effect” is not a key channel through which monetary policy actions influence economic outcomes.
claims.claim: Footnote 5: fast repricing of stocks and bonds does not speed transmission because liquid-asset wealth is concentrated among wealthier households and has small consumption effects.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: for the first time since the early 1990s central banks are beginning to face trade- offs between their employment and inflation objectives.
claims.claim: Central banks now face employment/inflation tradeoffs for the first time since the early 1990s: for decades hot inflation coincided with strong activity and low inflation with weak activity, so policy direction was unambiguous.
claims.conditions: Tradeoff regime: inflation above target while activity weakens

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Historically, central banks facing tradeoffs has been a catalyst for elevated macro uncertainty.
claims.claim: Tradeoffs cause abrupt policy changes and uncertainty about future policy (e.g. Volcker cut rates in 1980 as unemployment rose, then resumed hiking into a prolonged recession; March 2023 front-end volatility).

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: months in which core PCE inflation exceeded four percent (twice the Fed’s target) and unemployment was above the Congressional Budget Office estimate of NAIRU—JLN averaged 0.6 vs. -0.1 in all other months
claims.claim: Fed-tradeoff months (core PCE inflation > 4% and unemployment above CBO NAIRU) show mean JLN of 0.6 versus -0.1 in all other months.
claims.exact_rule: tradeoff month = core PCE inflation > 4% AND unemployment rate > CBO NAIRU estimate
claims.data_needed: Core PCE inflation, unemployment rate, CBO NAIRU, JLN index
claims.reported_result: JLN mean 0.6 (tradeoff months) vs -0.1 (other months); sample not stated

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: the difference- in-means is highly significant, with a t-stat in excess of seven
claims.claim: The difference in mean JLN between tradeoff and other months has a t-stat above 7.
claims.reported_result: t-stat > 7 (no autocorrelation adjustment mentioned; JLN is highly persistent so naive t-stat is likely overstated: reader note)
claims.conditions: Naive t-test on a series with 0.98 monthly autocorrelation

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: An additional catalyst for sustained elevated macro uncertainty is the degree to which markets and policymaker and economist forecasts disagree on the evolution of key macroeconomic variables: interest rates, inflation, and growth.
claims.claim: Disagreement between market pricing and policymaker/economist forecasts on rates, inflation and growth is a second driver of sustained uncertainty.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: All central banks, de facto if not de jure, strive for full employment and low inflation.
claims.claim: Footnote 6: even central banks with only a price-stability mandate (e.g. ECB) are not indifferent to unemployment, so tradeoffs apply broadly.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: and will cumulatively slash interest rates by roughly 2.25 percent over the next 18 months, culminating with a funds rate of around 3 percent at end of 2024.
claims.claim: On 3 May 2023 futures priced the May hike as the last, cuts from September, about 2.25 pts of cuts over 18 months to about 3% at end-2024.
claims.data_needed: Fed funds futures curve (Bloomberg); FOMC SEP
claims.reported_result: Futures-implied funds rate path as of May 3 2023: about 2.25 pt cut over 18 months, about 3% at end 2024; read from Figure 2 LHS: curve falls from about 5.1% to about 2.8% by 2025

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: At the beginning of March, it was pricing a peak funds rate of nearly 6 percent, and a funds rate of 4.25 percent at the end of 2024.
claims.claim: Futures pricing was very volatile: early March peak funds rate nearly 6% and 4.25% at end-2024, versus about 3% by May 3; author reads front-end volatility as evidence of elevated economic uncertainty.
claims.reported_result: Early March: peak near 6%, end-2024 4.25%; Figure 2 LHS shows Jan 18, Mar 8 and May 3 curves (Mar 8 peaks about 5.7%, May 3 about 5.1%)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: While the market believes the tightening cycle is over and rate cuts are imminent, all FOMC members and over 70 percent of economists surveyed by the Financial Times
claims.claim: Market pricing (cuts imminent) disagrees with all FOMC members and over 70% of surveyed economists, who forecast zero cuts in 2023; the gap is the largest since the SEP began in 2012.
claims.reported_result: All FOMC members and >70% of FT-surveyed economists forecast zero 2023 cuts; SEP March 22 2023 dots about 5.1% (2023), 4.1% (2024), 3.1% (2025) vs futures about 4.0% end-2024 (read from chart)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: The disparity between FOMC projections and futures market pricing is the largest observed since the SEP began in 2012.
claims.claim: The FOMC-versus-futures gap is the widest since the Summary of Economic Projections began in 2012.
claims.reported_result: Largest gap since 2012 (SEP start)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Either the FOMC and forecasters are right and interest rate expectations get re-priced, or the futures market is right and Federal Reserve credibility erodes.
claims.claim: Disagreement must be resolved either by market repricing or by loss of Fed credibility; either way volatility and macro uncertainty stay high.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Inflation-linked bond markets forecast inflation returning to two percent over the next year and staying there for the next decade.
claims.claim: Breakevens imply inflation at about 2% for the next decade while consensus forecasts expect more gradual disinflation (about 3.9% in year 1 easing to about 2.5% at 10 years), with realized y/y inflation 5.0%.
claims.reported_result: Figure 2 RHS: realized y/y inflation 5.0%; breakevens about 2.0-2.2% flat across 1-10Y; consensus about 3.9% (1Y), about 3.2% (2Y), about 2.5% (10Y) (read from chart)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: If investors wish to insure themselves against a state of the world in which interest rates are lower (as might occur in a recession), they may be willing to pay a premium to hold a long futures position.
claims.claim: Footnote 9: part of the futures-versus-survey gap may be a negative risk premium (investors pay to hold long rate futures as recession insurance), so the gap is not purely disagreement.
claims.conditions: Weakens the reading of futures as pure forecasts

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Both market-based and survey-based long-run inflation expectations have remained quite well anchored during the recent inflation experience.
claims.claim: Footnote 10: long-run inflation expectations are anchored now, but a de-anchoring would make disinflation costlier (more weakness and unemployment) and could bring back an inflation risk premium in nominal bonds as in the 1980s (cites Brooks 2021, Ilmanen 2011 ch. 9).
claims.conditions: Risk if core inflation stays above target or re-emerges after a policy pivot

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: This is not the first time this hiking cycle futures markets have dramatically piled on bets of lower rates.
claims.claim: Footnote 7: earlier front-end rallies occurred after the surprisingly high June inflation print and the first disinflation signs last fall, i.e. futures repeatedly over-priced cuts in this cycle.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Perhaps interest rate futures and inflation markets are forecasting an imminent and dramatic slowdown in economic activity.
claims.claim: One way to reconcile bond/futures pricing with survey forecasts is an imminent sharp slowdown, which would hurt equities, yet equities show no evidence of pricing a slowdown (cross-asset disagreement).

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: the large amount of disagreement indicates that the economy is on a knife’s edge, and dissonant market pricing is a powder keg for higher volatility.
claims.claim: Author concludes large cross-market and market-vs-forecaster disagreement means higher volatility is likely, while stressing he is not saying either side is right.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: JLN is 0.6 correlated with VIX and 0.5 correlated with realized volatility.
claims.claim: JLN has a correlation of 0.6 with the VIX and 0.5 with 22-day realized equity volatility, so persistent macro uncertainty implies elevated market volatility.
claims.exact_rule: correlation of standardized JLN with standardized VIX and 22-day realized equity-market volatility
claims.data_needed: JLN; VIX; 22-day realized volatility of equity market (BLS, Fed, Bloomberg per source line)
claims.reported_result: Correlation 0.6 (VIX), 0.5 (22-day realized vol); sample not stated

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Figure 3 plots JLN against 22-day realized equity market volatility and the VIX index (all series standardized).
claims.claim: Figure 3 shows JLN, 22-day realized equity volatility and VIX as z-scores; spike together in 2008 and 2020.
claims.exact_rule: z-score each series, plot JLN, 22-day realized vol, VIX
claims.reported_result: Chart only (about 1965-2022): realized-vol z-score peaks about 8.8 (2008) and about 8.2 (2020); JLN peaks about 5.3 (2020) and about 3 (1980); read approximately

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: the fallout from the failures of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank are unlikely to spark a widespread financial crisis.
claims.claim: Footnote 11 (author's opinion): the March 2023 bank failures are unlikely to trigger a widespread crisis because of the Fed/Treasury liquidity response, real GDP forecasts revised up by 40 bp since end-February (Consensus Economics), and because systemic crises usually come from asset quality, not duration mismatch.
claims.reported_result: Real GDP growth forecasts revised up by average 40 bp since end-February 2023 (Consensus Economics)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: the level of uncertainty at the front end of the yield curve led the Silicon Valley Bank shock to cause to a massive re-pricing of monetary policy expectations and a spike in macro and market volatility more broadly.
claims.claim: Footnote 11: because front-end uncertainty was already high, the SVB shock produced a massive repricing of policy expectations and a volatility spike (March events 'conform to this narrative').

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: equity markets have tended to do poorly when macro uncertainty is elevated.
claims.claim: High-uncertainty periods tend to bring surprisingly high inflation or weak growth, hence poor equity returns; asset performance over intermediate horizons is tied to the economic regime.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: stocks were negative in both the 1970s (stagflation) and the 2000s (tech bust and global financial crisis).
claims.claim: Stocks had negative ten-year excess returns in the 1970s and 2000s, so macro headwinds can make decade-long equity losses 'not uncommon'.
claims.reported_result: Figure 4 Sharpe ratios (read from chart): 1970s stocks about -0.02, bonds about 0, commodities about 1.0, equal risk about 0.8; 2000s stocks about -0.12, bonds about 0.62, commodities about 0.32, equal risk about 0.42

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Figure 4 displays the Sharpe ratios of stocks, bonds, and commodities since 1970.
claims.claim: Sharpe ratios of stocks/bonds/commodities/equal-risk by decade: 1980s stocks about 0.6, bonds about 0.32, commodities about -0.22, ER about 0.4; 1990s about 0.48, 0.5, 0.02, 0.59; last 10 years about 0.6, 0.03, -0.1, 0.3; full sample 1970-2023 about 0.3, 0.35, 0.28, 0.52.
claims.data_needed: MSCI World; Bloomberg Barclays US Government Bond (Ibbotson intermediate before 1973); Bloomberg Commodity Index; ICE BofAML 3M T-bill as cash
claims.reported_result: Read from bar charts, approximate; full sample Sharpe: stocks about 0.3, bonds about 0.35, commodities about 0.28, equal risk about 0.52; as of 31 Mar 2023
claims.conditions: Asset-class performance differs sharply by macro decade

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: investors should diversify, at least partially, away from simple equity risk.
claims.claim: Given persistent uncertainty, investors should diversify away from pure equity: bonds hedge negative growth shocks, commodities hedge positive inflation shocks.
claims.direction: add bonds and commodities to equity

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: a simple “risk parity” portfolio in which the weight on each asset class is inversely proportional to its realized volatility—delivers much more consistent performance across macroeconomic environments than equities (or any single asset class).
claims.claim: An equal-risk portfolio (weights inversely proportional to realized volatility) of stocks, bonds and commodities has more consistent Sharpe across decades than any single asset (full sample about 0.52 vs 0.28-0.35).
claims.exact_rule: weight_i proportional to 1 / realized volatility_i, across stocks, bonds, commodities
claims.reported_result: Equal-risk Sharpe about 0.8 (1970s), 0.4 (1980s), 0.59 (1990s), 0.42 (2000s), 0.3 (last 10y), 0.52 (full); read from chart
claims.conditions: Realized-vol window, rebalancing and leverage not specified
claims.testable: partly - lookback of realized vol and leverage not given

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Stocks are defined as the MSCI World Index. Bonds are defined as the Bloomberg Barclays U.S. Government Bond Index and, prior to 1973, the Ibbotson U.S. Intermediate Government Bond Index. Commodities are defined as the Bloomberg Commodity Index.
claims.claim: Figure 4 asset proxies: MSCI World; Bloomberg Barclays US Government Bond (Ibbotson intermediate govt bond before 1973); Bloomberg Commodity Index; excess return over ICE BofAML 3-month T-bill, as of 31 March 2023.
claims.data_needed: MSCI World, Bloomberg Barclays US Govt Bond Index, Ibbotson US Intermediate Govt Bond (pre-1973), Bloomberg Commodity Index, ICE BofAML US 3M T-Bill

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: many long-short liquid alternative strategies have little sensitivity to the macroeconomic backdrop and can provide strong performance across a range of market environments.
claims.claim: Long-short liquid alternatives have little macro sensitivity and can perform across environments (asserted, no evidence shown).

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Trend-following strategies, which at their core profit from the systematic tendency of markets to gradually incorporate new information, tend to outperform when economic shocks are large and markets experience stress.
claims.claim: Trend following profits from gradual incorporation of information, so it tends to outperform when shocks are large and markets stressed.
claims.direction: long trend following in high-uncertainty regimes
claims.conditions: Works when economic shocks are large; 2010s low-volatility decade was weak for trend

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: The SG Trend index, an equal weighted average of the performance of the ten largest trend-following managers, has posted positive returns in the three largest equity market drawdowns since the inception of the index in 2000
claims.claim: SG Trend (equal-weighted ten largest CTAs, since 2000) was positive in the three largest equity drawdowns.
claims.data_needed: SG Trend Index (Bloomberg); MSCI World monthly returns
claims.reported_result: Figure 5: SG Trend vs MSCI World monthly returns in six drawdowns: Nov 2007-Feb 2009 about +22% vs about -53%; Apr 2000-Sep 2002 about +51% vs about -47%; Jan 2022-Sep 2022 about +35% vs about -25%; Jan 2020-Mar 2020 about +2.5% vs about -21%; Oct 2018-Dec 2018 about -5% vs about -13%; average +21.1% vs -32.1% (read from chart except labelled averages)
claims.conditions: Exhibit includes smaller 2018 drawdown where SG Trend lost about 5%; text mentions only the three largest

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: A more comprehensive approach to trend following that includes economic trends
claims.claim: Trend following that adds economic trends (Brooks et al 2023) and alternative markets (Babu et al 2020 'Trends Everywhere') may give more robust tail protection and better average returns than the SG Trend benchmark.
claims.direction: broaden trend to economic series and alternative markets
claims.testable: partly - evidence in cited papers, not here

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: the abundance of economic catalysts and cross-market dispersion
claims.claim: Global macro (heterogeneous) may benefit from high uncertainty via many economic catalysts and cross-market dispersion; Brooks (2017) macro momentum is cited as positively convex.
claims.conditions: Global macro is a heterogeneous category; only some strategies benefit

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Timing when you need diversification is a fool’s errand, and investors that do so typically find themselves the proverbial, “day late, dollar short.”
claims.claim: Diversification is recommended unconditionally; the author argues against timing it, though persistent uncertainty makes now an opportune moment to review portfolios.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Figures shown are based on monthly returns. Past performance is not a guarantee of future performance.
claims.claim: Figure 5 uses monthly returns, so peak-to-trough drawdown windows are measured on month-end data.
